speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) why do investments bought using the CPF Special Account or Ordinary Account of a deceased member go to his estate upon death and not to his CPF nominee; and (b) whether the CPF will consider allowing such investments to also go to the nominee rather than the estate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These decisions should be made by the beneficiaries, as these decisions could affect the value of the CPFIS investments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the issue arises particularly with vulnerable families or less-educated individuals and the CPF Nomination Scheme was meant to be an easy way to avoid people having to write wills if their only asset was CPF.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, for example, if an individual is bankrupt, his CPF monies would go to his nominee, which could be the wife.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But if it were to go to the estate, it would all go to the creditors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had a Meet-the-People Session (MPS) case, for example, where a bankrupt had CPF monies which could not be touched by the creditors, which he was hoping to go to the wife, but because they had gone into investments, they went to the creditors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second, is again bankruptcy, but, where one of the recipients is a bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this case, the nominee was the wife, but, because the money were in investments, they went to the estate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There was no will, so half of it would go to a child, who happened to be a bankrupt; and the other half would go to the wife.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But then, the creditors then come in to decide how to sell the assets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another solution may be, to have the assets go to the nominee and then the nominee can decide when to sell, because the beneficiary and the estate may be quite different from the nominee.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because, at the particular point in time, the Government took a stand at that time, as far as possible in terms of the growth, for the economy, we wanted to benefit a larger part of a group of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When it comes to managing the investments, I think that it would not be prudent for CPF to manage the timing of the sale of these assets because, ostensibly for us, it is really to protect the member and his nominees to provide for financial retirement adequacy; and also to help them with the MediSave and also for housing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you try to manage and disburse the investment proceeds and time the sale of the investment that the member has made and you make a wrong timing or you make a wrong a decision to sell or, well, you made a decision to sell but at a wrong timing, it could have adverse impact on the savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because of that, we left it to the beneficiaries according to the will.
